identity.title: RM-Bench: Benchmarking Reward Models of Language Models with Subtlety and Style

problem.claim: Reward models must guide alignment and response selection, but their evaluation should capture sensitivity to subtle content changes and style variation.

gap.claim: Existing benchmarks often compare responses from models of different power, overlooking subtle content and style effects and showing low correlation with policy-model performance.

contributions.claim: Introduces RM-Bench for evaluating sensitivity to subtle content differences and resistance to style biases.
Evaluates nearly 40 reward models and reports their performance under subtlety and style-bias conditions.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors characterize RM-Bench as a novel benchmark distinguished by its focus on subtle content differences and resistance to style biases.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that RM-Bench strongly correlates with policy-model performance and serves as a reference for reward-model selection.
The authors report that even state-of-the-art reward models average 46.6% under style-bias interference, below the stated 50% random-level accuracy.

narrative_sequence.summary: Reward models are used to guide language-model alignment and select responses.
Common benchmarks emphasize distinguishing outputs from models of varying power, missing subtle content and style effects.
RM-Bench is introduced to test subtle-content sensitivity and resistance to style bias.
Nearly 40 reward models are evaluated; the authors report correlation with policy performance and substantial weakness under style bias.

source_observation.claim: The abstract links benchmark performance to policy-model performance while separately exposing style-bias interference.

lessons.interpretation: Evaluation can be more informative when its test dimensions reflect downstream use and isolate specific failure modes.
lessons.application: Design benchmark splits that separately test task-relevant judgment and systematic nuisance biases, then report their relationship to downstream performance.
lessons.exception: This framing may be unsuitable when the target application has no identifiable downstream metric or relevant nuisance variation.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the correlation metric, benchmark construction, model identities, or evaluation protocol.
It does not state whether the 46.6% versus 50% difference is statistically significant or how style-bias interference is operationalized.
